newsitem.title: INDIA: Indian panel clears Tata-SIA airline.
newsitem.headline: Indian panel clears Tata-SIA airline.

text.p: A plan by India's Tata group and Singapore Airlines Ltd (SIA) to set up a domestic Indian airline has cleared a major government hurdle, sparking an outcry among communists and Hindu nationalists.

A senior government official and industry sources said on Tuesday the Foreign Investment Promotion Board (FIPB) had recently cleared the two-year-old project and sent it to Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda's cabinet for a final decision.
The FIPB is made up of senior government officials.
Industry sources said the Cabinet Committee on Foreign Investment was expected to take a decision later in January.
In February 1995, SIA and Tata Industries Ltd submitted their proposal to launch the airline. The Tatas were planning to hold a 60 percent stake, with SIA owning the rest.
Since then, the proposal has languished in the government, ensnared in a high-stakes battle over whether to permit foreign investment in the civil aviation sector.
Tata Industries vice president S. Ramakrishnan said his firm would remain cautious until final approval.
"It's definitely a positive step but we still have other steps to go through," Ramakrishnan said. "Ultimately we need an approval in writing."

India began opening its aviation sector as part of an economic liberalisation programme launched under then prime minister P.V. Narasimha Rao in 1991. But Civil Aviation Minister C.M. Ibrahim has fought a high-profile campaign to protect the state-owned airlines -- Indian Airlines on domestic routes and Air-India on international routes -- from foreign competition.
Last year the Civil Aviation Ministry began reviewing policy regarding foreign equity stakes in domestic airlines.

Currently the government reviews foreign companies' proposals on a case-by-case basis. If approved, a foreign firm can take up to a 40 percent stake in a domestic airline. Gulf Air and Kuwait Airways each have stakes in India's Jet Airways.
On Tuesday, the Financial Express quoted Ibrahim as saying a new civil aviation policy being drafted by the government would bar foreign firms from taking an equity stake in domestic airlines.
Ibrahim's campaign has irritated free traders in Deve Gowda's 13-party centre-left coalition. But his drive has the backing of communists, who support the government.

The Communist Party of India-Marxist (CPI-M) said the FIPB's move was at odds with Ibrahim's position. The CPI-M politburo released a statement saying the joint venture "would be a major departure from the policy so far adopted...There is no reason whatsoever for this policy to be changed".
The main opposition Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) joined the communists in criticising the FIPB's move.
"The BJP is totally opposed to any kind of (foreign) equity participation in the civil aviation sector," BJP leader Pramod Mahajan told Reuters.
"We don't mind the Tatas coming into this sector on their own but we are against Singapore Airlines entering the domestic sector," he said.

Mahajan said the finance and industry ministries appeared to have cleared the project without consulting civil aviation. "If the civil aviation ministry stands upright and refuses to approve the project, it will not go through," he said.
